content.text: Dhruva, son of King Uttanapada by his queen Suniti, saw his half-brother Uttama seated on their father's lap and wished to climb up too; but the favourite queen Suruchi, present at the time, rebuked him before the court: ‘Why, child, do you vainly indulge in such presumptuous hopes? You are born from a different mother... This regal throne... is suited to my son only; why should you aspire to its occupation?’
content.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XI & XII

content.text: Dhruva, in tears, ran to his mother Suniti, who, deeply distressed, told him: ‘Suruchi has rightly spoken; thine, child, is an unhappy fate... a wise man will be contented with that degree which appertains to him.’ But Dhruva answered her: ‘Mother, the words that you have addressed to me for my consolation find no place in a heart that contumely has broken. I will exert myself to obtain such elevated rank, that it shall be revered by the whole world... I wish for no other honours than such as my own actions shall acquire, such as even my father has not enjoyed.’
content.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XI & XII

content.text: Dhruva then quitted the city and entered a forest, where he found seven Munis seated on antelope hides. He told them he sought a station no one before him had attained. The sage Marichi said, ‘The best of stations is not within the reach of men who fail to propitiate Govinda. Do thou, prince, worship the undecaying.’ The Rishis taught him the prayer: ‘Om! glory to Vasudeva, whose essence is divine wisdom; whose form is inscrutable, or is manifest as Brahma, Vishnu, and Siva’ — the same prayer, they told him, once uttered by his own grandsire Manu Swayambhuva.
content.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XI & XII

content.text: As Dhruva's mind became wholly absorbed in meditation at Madhuvana on the Yamuna, the earth itself could not sustain the weight of his asceticism, and the gods, alarmed, sent illusions to distract him: an apparition of his weeping mother begging him to desist, then hideous Rakshasas and monsters roaring to terrify him. But 'all these uncouth spectres, appalling cries, and threatening weapons, made no impression upon his senses, whose mind was completely intent on Govinda.'
content.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XI & XII

content.text: Unable to shake him, the gods appealed to Vishnu himself, who at last appeared to the boy in person, four-armed, bearing the shell, discus, mace, bow, and scimetar, and touched him with the tip of his conch-shell. Overwhelmed, Dhruva praised him: ‘I venerate him whose forms are earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect... Salutation to that spirit that is void of qualities... My heart is overflowing with devotion to thee: oh lord, grant me the faculty worthily to lay mine adorations at thy feet.’
content.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XI & XII

content.text: Vishnu asked Dhruva to name his boon, and the boy confessed his original, prideful motive honestly: ‘The sister-queen of my mother has said to me, loudly and arrogantly, “The royal throne is not for one who is not born of me;” and I now solicit of the support of the universe an exalted station, superior to all others, and one that shall endure for ever.’ Vishnu did not rebuke the ambition but granted it: ‘The station that thou askest thou shalt obtain; for I was satisfied with thee of old in a prior existence.’
content.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XI & XII

content.text: Vishnu granted Dhruva a station above the sun, the moon, and all the constellations, to sustain the stars and planets for the duration of a Kalpa, with his mother Suniti abiding near him as a companion star. ‘Wonderful is the efficacy of this penance, marvellous is its reward, that the seven Rishis should be preceded by Dhruva,’ declared Usanas, preceptor of the gods — and to this day Dhruva is identified with the fixed pole star.
content.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XI & XII
